name: Gel manicure

lead: A gel manicure uses a polish that stays tacky until cured under a UV or LED lamp. Several thin layers are cured one at a time, producing a hard, glossy finish that resists chipping far better than ordinary polish.

The appearance payoff is tidy, even-coloured nails for an extended period. Wikipedia describes gel as similarly durable and complex in design to acrylic nails, and as more costly than traditional polish.

paras: The process is done in a salon or at home with a lamp: nails are prepared, base, colour and top coats are applied and cured, and the polish is later removed with a dedicated removal procedure. People use it for events, travel or low-maintenance grooming.

A 2026 review of 28 studies found brittleness and splitting to be the most common side effects, with allergic contact dermatitis reported in six publications and rare squamous cell carcinoma cases linked to UV lamps. The review concluded that health risks are limited and called for more research on UV exposure limits.

Coat stays glossy and chip-resistant for weeks
angle.text: A gel manicure gives nails an even, glossy colour that lasts through everyday use, so hands look groomed without frequent redoing.

lead: A gel manicure applies gel polish, also sold as hybrid or shellac-style polish, in layers that are each cured under a UV or LED lamp [1]. Gel stays tacky until cured, unlike acrylic, which dries on its own [1].

People use it to keep nails looking finished and uniform for weeks. Wikipedia describes gel nails as comparable to acrylic in durability and design complexity, with traditional polish chipping more easily, and notes gel can cost more [1].

Research on gel manicures covers nail plate changes, allergy and UV exposure. A review following PRISMA guidelines found 28 studies from 2011 to 2024 and concluded UV-cured manicures pose limited health risks [2].

paras: Manicurists apply several layers of gel and cure each under a lamp [1]. A variant called cat eye gel polish contains magnetically responsive particles that a magnet orients before curing fixes the pattern [1].
Gel is described as similarly durable to acrylic and more chip-resistant than traditional polish [1].

A 2026 review reported brittleness and splitting as the most common side effects, allergic contact dermatitis in six publications, and single reports of paronychia and pterygium inversum unguis. Rare squamous cell carcinoma cases were linked to UV lamps, though most studies suggest minimal cancer risk [2].

Case reports describe psoriasis-like nail changes after at-home gel manicures and after photobonded acrylic nails; one case improved with topical and intralesional steroids [3][4]. A 3D scanning study of 20 thumb nails found that manicure procedures changed the nail plate structure, which the authors linked to acetone, filing and applied substances [5]. A letter in JAAD Case Reports responded to a report of dermatomyositis triggered by UV gel nail lamp exposure [6].

Research is mostly reviews and case reports. The 2026 review found limited health risks and called for more work on application guidelines and UV limits [2]. A randomized controlled trial of 17 volunteers examined pulse oximetry readings with gel manicures in several colours [7].
